name: Forward head posture exercises

card.summary: Neck-strengthening and chin-tuck style routines for forward head posture; studied for neck pain, with community debate over whether they help or hurt the profile.
card.aka: Chin tucks, neck strengthening, tech neck exercises
card.note: Studies link forward head posture and neck pain, but the association is not uniform and cosmetic effects are unstudied.

quick.overview:
Forward head posture (FHP, also called nerd neck or tech neck) is when the head sits ahead of the shoulders. Exercise routines for it usually aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and upper back and stretch tight muscles at the neck and chest.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed both as a way to improve profile and posture and as something that might make a recessed chin look worse once the head is pulled back. Research focuses on neck pain and headache, not looks.
quick.mechanism: FHP is quantified by the craniovertebral angle. Exercise programmes target the deep cervical flexors and scapular muscles, and a trial found neck exercises improved the ability of people with chronic neck pain to hold an upright posture during a task.
quick.risks: Exercise itself is generally low risk, but the sources reviewed do not establish that exercise permanently changes head position or appearance. Evidence linking FHP to pain is mixed, with a meta-analysis finding an association in adults but not adolescents.

lead: Forward head posture (FHP) is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, often accompanied by rounded shoulders and increased upper-back curvature. It is commonly called text neck, tech neck or nerd neck, and is measured clinically with the craniovertebral angle [1][2]. Exercises for it typically aim to strengthen the deep neck flexors and shoulder-blade retractors and to stretch tight neck and chest muscles [3].

Research has examined the association of FHP with neck pain and headache and tested exercise regimens in people with neck pain [4][5][6]. A systematic review and meta-analysis found a relationship between FHP and neck pain in adults [7].

In looksmaxxing forums, FHP is discussed as affecting side-profile and overall posture, and some users argue that correcting it can make a recessed chin look weaker. No published study has examined these appearance claims.
infobox: Forward head posture, upper crossed pattern

paras: Wikipedia describes FHP as a hunched, kyphotic upper spine with the head carried forward, common among people who spend long hours at devices and in certain occupations [3]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes measurement by the craniovertebral angle, with values below 50 degrees taken to indicate FHP, and repeats a widely cited estimate that load on the neck rises as the head moves forward [1]. The upper crossed pattern combines tight upper trapezius, levator scapulae and pectoral muscles with weak deep neck flexors [1].

Programmes commonly described include strengthening the deep neck flexors and mid and lower back muscles, stretching the upper trapezius and chest, breaks from sustained postures, and ergonomic changes [3]. Thoracic manipulation has also been studied for neck pain [3].
A trial of 58 people compared two neck-exercise regimens for the ability of people with chronic neck pain to maintain an upright cervical and thoracic posture during a distracting task [5].

A cross-sectional study of 62 people with neck pain and 52 without examined head posture measured by the craniovertebral angle in relation to pain and disability [4]. Older studies reported differences in head posture and upper cervical flexor performance in people with cervical headache and in tension-type headache and migraine [8][9][10].
A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis examined the relationship between forward head posture and neck pain [7]. Wikipedia summarises it as finding a link in adults but not adolescents [3].

An observational study of office workers compared neck and shoulder postures between symptomatic and asymptomatic people [11], and an earlier study examined postural abnormalities and pain in healthy adults [12]. No studies found testing whether FHP exercises change facial appearance, jaw or chin profile.

One looksmax.org thread suggests FHP is common among models and actors and asks whether correcting it is unnecessary; a reply says they may pose that way for photos, and another user wonders about links to maxillary growth after gaming through adolescence [13]. Another thread cites an article on health problems associated with FHP and reports that good head posture becomes natural over time [14]. A third argues that people with a recessed chin or jaw hold the head forward to open the airway, and that tucking the chin back makes the chin look worse [15].
Proponents of correction cite pain and posture; those wary of it cite profile aesthetics. The sources reviewed do not test either position.

lore.intro: Forum discussion of forward head posture splits between those who treat it as a flaw to fix and those who question whether fixing it helps looks [13][14][15].

claims.claim: Forward head posture causes problems throughout the body.
claims.believers: A thread presents FHP as harming the whole body and says it feels natural after a period of good posture [14].
claims.experts: Studies associate FHP with neck pain and headache in some groups, though a meta-analysis found the link in adults but not adolescents [3][7].

claims.claim: Fixing forward head posture makes a recessed chin look worse.
claims.believers: A user says a chin tuck leaves him with almost no visible chin and asks whether correcting posture is worthwhile [15].
claims.experts: No published study has examined how head position changes chin appearance in the context of exercise.

claims.claim: Forward head posture may affect maxillary growth.
claims.believers: A user wonders whether years of gaming with forward head posture affected his forward-grown maxilla [13].
claims.experts: The sources reviewed contain no studies on head posture and maxillary growth.

claims.claim: Models and actors have forward head posture, so correcting it may be unnecessary.
claims.believers: A thread asks whether correction is 'cope', with a reply saying they pose that way for photos [13].
claims.experts: No study found testing attractiveness ratings of head posture.
